1
INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici are uniquely positioned to address the impact
on public safety of AR-15 platform rifles and similar semiautomatic weapons. They collectively represent over 300
years of law enforcement experience at the local, state,
and federal levels, including as police commissioners and
chief executives in New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago,
Philadelphia, the District of Columbia , Boston, Buffalo,
Seattle, and Milwaukee. They have led their departments
through mass shootings and terrorist attacks, improved
community relations, built public trust, and helped lead
and train thousands of officers who are charged with
maintaining safety and order in America ’s cities. Amici
know how difficult the job of law enforcement is and have
dedicated their careers to protecting the public and their
officers. They can speak from firsthand experience to the
unique dangers posed by  AR-15s and similar semiautomatic weapons, as well as the reasons a state or local legislature would sensibly want to keep those extraordinarily
powerful weapons off the streets.
* Amicus William J. Bratton  has more than fifty
years of law enforcement experience. Over his long career
of service, Commissioner Bratton has commanded six police departments, including the New York City Police Department, the Los Angeles Police Department, and the
Boston Police Department. He is the only person ever to
have led the police departments of the N ation’s two largest cities.

1 No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in part.
No entity or person, aside from amic i curiae or their counsel, made
any monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation or submission of this brief.

2
* Amicus Gil Kerlikowske has built a wide -ranging
and extensive law enforcement career  over forty years.
He was Chief of Police in Seattle from 2000 to 2009, Police
Commissioner in Buffalo from 1995 to 1998, and was twice
elected President of the Major Cities Chiefs  Association.
He later became the first permanent U.S. Commissioner
of Customs and Border Protection from 2014 to 2017. He
also served as Director of the Office of National Drug
Control Policy from 2009 to 2014.
* Amicus Charlie Beck  is a former Chief of the Los
Angeles Police Department. A department veteran with
over four decades as an officer, he is known for commanding and rehabilitating the Rampart Division after the
Rampart scandal, and for implementing technological enhancements during his time as Chief of Detectives. He
served as interim Superintendent of Police in Chicago in
2019.
* Amicus Edward Flynn ’s career spans forty -five
years (thirty years as a chief executive) in four S tates,
during which he led six different agencies. His police career concluded with ten years of service as Milwaukee Police Chief. His prior positions included service as P olice
Commissioner in Springfield, Massachusetts; as Massachusetts Secretary of Public Safety; and as Arlington
County, Virginia, Police Chief, where he led police recovery efforts at the Pentagon on September 11, 2001.
* Amicus Ed Davis has worked in law enforcement for
thirty-five years and is a recognized expert in community
policing and public safety. He served as the Police Commissioner of the City of Boston from December 2006 until
October 2013. He led the highly successful response to the
Boston Marathon bombing. Before  that, Commissioner
Davis was the Superintendent of the Lowell Police De-

3
partment, a position he held for twelve years. His law enforcement career began as a patrol officer in 1978.
* Amicus Kathleen M. O ’Toole started her career in
law enforcement in 1979 as a Boston police officer. In the
nearly five decades since, she has served as the Massachusetts Secretary of Public Safety, the Commissioner of
the Boston Police Department, the Chief Inspector of Ireland’s Garda Inspectorate, and most recently as Seattle’s
first female Chief of Police. She holds a Ph. D. from the
Business School of Trinity College Dublin.
* Amicus Charles Ramsey , former Commissioner of
the Philadelphia Police Department, has forty -five years
of law enforcement experience and expertise. Before leading the Philadelphia Police Department in 2008, he served
as Deputy Superintendent of the Chicago Police Department in 1994 and as Chief of the Metropolitan Police Department of the District of Columbia from 1998 to 2007.
In 2017, he became a regular CNN contributor.
* Amicus James ( Jim) Pugel began his career with
the Seattle Police Department in 1983. In 2014, a fter
thirty-one years with the department, he retired as Chief
of Police. He then served as the Chief Deputy of the King
County, Washington, Sheriff’s Office from 2014 to 2018.
He now regularly serves as an expert witness in policerelated litigation.
* Amicus Kim C. Dine has worked in law enforcement
for over forty years. He began his career with the Metropolitan Police Department of the District of Columbia in
1975, retiring in 2002 as an A ssistant Chief. He then
served as Chief of the Frederick, Maryland,  Police Department for ten years, before returning to Washington
in 2012 to serve as Chief of the United States Capitol Police until 2016.

4
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Amici have devoted their careers to leading the brave
law enforcement officers who serve on the front lines protecting their communities . As police chiefs  and commissioners, the ir job was to  keep both the  public and the
officers who serve it safe. The proliferation of AR-15 platform weapons2 is antithetical to both missions. Amici’s experience leads them to a well -informed and deeply held
view that state and local legislatures ’ ability to impose
reasonable regulations on possession of these particularly
deadly weapons is imperative to protecting  law enforcement officers and civilians alike.
I. AR-15s in the hands of criminals pose a tremendous
danger to law enforcement  officers and the populations
they serve.
A. The lethal risks posed by these powerful semiautomatic rifles overwhelm standard police gear. The particularly potent features of AR-15 platform rifles combine into
an especially deadly weapon that can be (and often is)
trained at law enforcement  officers—to devastating effect. The rounds from these weapons travel significantly
farther, faster, and more accurately than handgun fire.
And because standard police equipment does not protect
against the rounds of an AR -15, these features can force
officers to delay engaging with a suspect until backup arrives with the necessary weapons and protective gear. Officers confronted by an AR -15 must therefore make an

2 The laws at issue in this case regulate  only a subset of semiautomatic rifles. As Respondents have explained, the weapons at issue
are commonly referred to as “assault weapons,” although they are
more precisely defined in the relevant laws under review. See Connecticut Respondents Br. 3–4; Cook County Respondents Br.  8. For
clarity, Amici will refer to these rifles as either AR -15 platform or
similar weapons, or—for the sake of brevity—AR-15s.

5
impossible choice: either challenge the shooter at great
risk to their own safety or spend precious time waiting for
necessary reinforcements.
B. Countless real -world examples of mass shooters,
terrorists, and criminals targeting police officers demonstrate that the ability of AR-15s to penetrate police armor
at long distances costs law enforcement and civilian lives.
Time after time, officers are unprotected and outgunned
when a shooter wields an AR -15 platform weapon. Precisely because heroic officers nevertheless risk their lives
to protect their communities even when their equipment
is outmatched,  scores of officers have been needlessly
killed by mass shooters and terrorists with AR-15s.
II. The prevalent criminal use of AR-15 platform rifles
also creates a deeply unfortunate dynamic that can only
be described as an arms race. If dangerous criminals have
easy access to weapons that can so readily  overpower
standard police equipment, then law enforcement agencies often have no choice but to increasingly arm themselves to patrol the communities they serve. Although
that may be necessary to protect officers ’ immediate
safety, the resulting impression of a more heavily armed
police force  strains relationships with the public. But
those relationships with the community are imperative to
successful policing: they allow law enforcement officers to
understand community conditions, engage with community leaders, keep peaceful protesters safe, and develop
proactive solutions to crime. Those imperatives become
impossible when officers must carry military -grade
shields, helmets that conceal their faces, and long guns—
all to protect against AR-15s.
The Court should affirm the judgments of the Second
and Seventh Circuits.

6
ARGUMENT
AR-15s overpower standard police equipment, leading
to an untenable situation on the ground for law enforcement officers.  See Connecticut Respondents  Br. 31–32;
Cook County Respondents Br. 31–36. The proliferation of
these weapons spawns a vicious cycle that endangers police officers and civilians alike; p olice forces are incentivized to arm and protect themselves against this ever -
present threat, but the intimidating and depersonalizing
equipment required to do so hinders their  relationships
with the communities they serve.
I. AR-15 platform rifles pose unique dangers to law
enforcement officers.
An officer’s job is dangerous enough as it is. Several
characteristics of AR-15s make it far more so. Legislators
should not be constitutionally kneecapped from enacting
commonsense regulations to make police work safer.
A. AR-15s overpower standard police equipment and
expose law enforcement officers to extraordinary
danger.
A police officer carries a standard kit. Her primary
weapon is a semiautomatic service pistol, typically a  .40-
caliber or 9mm handgun. 3 Under her uniform shirt , she
wears concealable lightweight soft body armor, rated to

3 Police Exec. Rsch. F., BJA /PERF Body Armor National Survey: Phase II Final Report 18 (2009) (“PERF Survey”) (listing these
as the “caliber of the primary firearm issued or authorized for officer
use by the majority of agencies”) ; cf. Expert Report of  James E.
Yurgealitis 29, Viramontes v. Cook County, No. 21-cv-4595 (N.D. Ill.
Mar. 3, 2023), ECF No. 81- 5 (“Yurgealitis Report”) (describing the
Sig Sauer P229 in .40 S&W issued to expert as an ATF agent).

7
stop handgun rounds.4 That equipment has been tailored
to meet the threats officers have historically faced 5—but
it is no match for an AR-15.
No single feature of AR-15s is unique; other centerfire
rifles share many of them. The  particular danger comes
from how the features combine. An AR-15 fires a high-velocity projectile that can cause far more serious wounds
than a comparably  sized handgun bullet. Th e rifle’s projectile can pierce the soft armor that most officers wear.
The rifle can deliver accurate fire well beyond the distances at which a  police officer’s pistol is effective. And
because the rifle is semiautomatic, has little recoil, and
feeds from a detachable magazine, the shooter can deliver
well-aimed shots in rapid succession. Each of these traits
makes the others more dangerous . Together, they leave
an officer equipped for an ordinary shift seriously outmatched.
1. Any bullet that strikes a vital organ can kill. But the
ammunition AR-15s most commonly fire, 5.56mm or .223,
is especially dangerous because of its velocity, the energy
it carries, and how that energy is released inside the
body.6 Rounds fired from a typical AR- 15 have a muzzle
velocity nearly three times faster than a 9mm pistol car-

4 PERF Survey, supra n.3, at 22 (survey conducted in 2007; 41.4
percent of agencies reported Level II and 35.0  percent Level IIIA
armor, designed to protect against handgun rounds).
5 Id. at 12-13 (explaining that 605 of 769 officers killed with firearms from 1985 to 1996 were killed with handguns).
6 See, e.g., Peter M. Rhee et al., Gunshot Wounds: A Review of

8
tridge.7 Once fired, these rifle projectiles likewise travel
two to three times faster than typical handgun projectiles.8 A round fired from an AR-15 thus carries “a larger
amount of kinetic energy, which after contact * * * is
transmitted to [surrounding] tissues.”9
An AR-15 bullet thus delivers far more devastating
wounds than one fired from a typical handgun. A handgun
bullet “generally travel[s] in a relatively straight line ”
through the body. 10 But an AR- 15’s 5.56mm bullet that
strikes tissue tends to “yaw,” rotating on its axis, which
contributes to “both temporary and permanent large
wound cavities.”11 A permanent wound cavity is the track
of tissue the bullet itself crushes and tears. A temporary
cavity is a short -lived, violent expansion of tissue pushed
outward from that track. 12 In high-velocity rifle wounds,
“the expanding walls of the temporary cavity are capable
of doing severe damage. ”13 Injuries can occur “to blood

distance from the path.”14 Put simply, critical organs that
are not even struck by a 5. 56mm or .223 bullet can be severely injured.
Fragmentation of the bullet upon impact can compound these effects . A “jacketed” bullet breaks apart in
soft tissue if it strikes at a sufficiently high velocity —as
the 5.56mm projectile fired by an AR-15 often does.15 The
resulting wounds often  require multiple operations and
massive transfusions where a comparable handgun wound
would not.16
2. Law enforcement officers are typically equipped to
defend themselves only against handguns. This leaves officers exposed to extraordinary danger when they encounter criminals armed with rifles  that can overpower
standard defensive gear.
The mismatch is starkest in body armor. The National
Institute of Justice rates armor by the ammunition that it
is certified to stop. The  “highest level of protection available for concealable wear ”—and the armor most commonly worn by officers while on duty —protects only
against “handgun threats.”17 Rifle protection begins at a

with some fragments which act as secondary projectiles causing further damage particularly to vascular structures.”).

15 Stefanopoulos, supra n.7, at 3 ( “Fracture of the jacket  * * * is
considered a characteristic feature of, although not limited to, the
5.56[mm round]. * * * The projectile depends on this [fragmentation]
mechanism for maximum effectiveness.”).
16 See, e.g., Stefanopoulos, supra n.7, at 7.

10
higher rating , which is “[i]ntended  for” limited “tactical
situations.”18
Meanwhile, “[m]ost agencies do not issue * * *  body
armor that protects against rifle or armor -piercing bullets” “for everyday wear.”19
Officer fatality data sadly reflects this. Rifles are overwhelmingly responsible for officer fatalities caused by armor-piercing bullets. Between 1985 and 2005, 78 percent
of officers killed by gunshot wounds that penetrated their
armor died from rifle rounds , “which the armor was not
designed to protect against. ”20 Likewise, from 2007 to
2016, armor-penetrating deaths were “mostly by rifle
rounds which exceeded the vest ’s specifications or rating.”21
This mismatch between standard -issue body armor
and AR-15s played out to tragic effect for  Douglas
County, Colorado,  Deputy Zach Parrish on New Year ’s
Eve 2017. Deputy Parrish responded in his standard-issue
“pistol-resistant” vest to reports of a mentally  ill individual holed up inside his apartment . When the subject
opened fire with a semiautomatic rifle, the bullets pierced
both a wall and Deputy Parrish’s body armor (twice), killing him. Deputy Parrish’s sheriff acknowledged that none

of his deputies’ vests “met the federal standard set to stop
rifle rounds. ” And a  neighboring sheriff explained why

Rifle-resistant ceramic plates are “an expensive addition”
to standard soft armor.22
Many agencies keep rif le-rated armor for tactical
teams and planned high-risk operations.23 But most officers do not and cannot reasonably wear it through an ordinary shift . Agencies also prefer concealable armor
because it lets officers “appear more approachable” than
externally worn armor, “which appear[s] more militaristic.”24
But active shooters and terrorist attacks arrive without warning. O fficers like Deputy Parrish answering a
disturbance call, or those who are the first to arrive at an
active shooting, must face the threat wearing the equipment that their standard shift requires.25 That defensive
gear is simply no match for an AR-15.
3. Rifle fire also threatens officers from distances that
their weapons cannot answer. C ommon service pistols
have an effective range of about 50 yards, and typical law
enforcement training emphasizes encounters between 3

22 Halsne & Koeberl, supra n.21.
23 See PERF Survey, supra n.3, at 22-23 & n.23.
24 PERF Survey, supra n.3, at 9.
25 See Scott W. Phillips, Myths, Militarism and the Police Patrol
Rifle, 26 P OLICING & SOCIETY 185, 186 (2016)  (patrol officers are
“first responders” to sudden active-shooter emergencies).

12
and 10 yards. 26 An AR-15, meanwhile,  has an effective
range of roughly 600 yards.27
That gap matters. Active shootings happen in parking
lots, school corridors, open plazas, and concert grounds,
where the distance between shooter and responder can
easily exceed the range at which an officer can reliably return fire with a pistol. Distance , ordinarily one of an officer’s most important protections, offers far less safety
against a rifle. Moving closer to engage means crossing
exposed ground under fire, while holding back to look for
cover means ceding precious time to the shooter. There is
simply no good choice when faced with a shooter armed
with an AR-15.
4. An AR-15’s semiautomatic firing feature, easy customization, and large ammunition capacity further compound the weapon’s lethality.
A semiautomatic rifle fires one round with each pull of
the trigger and reloads itself, using energy from the shot
to chamber the next round without any manual action  to
reload.28 That separates it from a fully automatic weapon,
which fires continuously while the trigger is held. It also
separates it from a bolt -action rifle, which requires the
shooter to work the action by hand between shots.29
Perhaps counterintuitively , semiautomatic firing
makes the AR- 15 more dangerous to officers than even

23-cv-209 (S.D. Ill. May 10, 2024), ECF No. 185-2 (“Barnett Report”).

861.

fully automatic weapons. Sustained, fully automatic fire
sacrifices accuracy. Semiautomatic fire lets the shooter
aim each shot. For this reason, the U.S. Army’s field manual calls semiautomatic fire the “most important firing
technique during fast -moving, modern combat, ” and observes that “[i]t is surprising how devastatingly accurate
rapid semiautomatic fire can be.”30
The AR-15’s low recoil reinforces that capability. As
Petitioners themselves have noted, AR- 15s are “easy to
shoot [with] little recoil. ”31 For a responding officer, this
means the shooter can bring the rifle back on target
quickly after each shot; a hunting rifle’s heavier recoil, by
contrast, typically forces the shooter to take more time “to
re-aim after each shot.”32
An AR-15 user can even further customize the weapon
to increase its accuracy. A pistol grip helps stabilize the
weapon during rapid fire and makes it easier to fire from
the hip, and a barrel shroud lets the shooter grasp the barrel area without being burned as it heats during sustained
fire.33 And criminals can easily increase a mmunition capacity to substantially amplify the AR-15’s effectiveness.
It is thus no surprise that many mass public shootings involved a large-capacity magazine (i.e., those with a capac-

II. The proliferation of AR-15 platform rifles forces
police into an unfortunate arms race—straining
relationships with communities and hindering law
enforcement efforts.
Law enforcement is not primarily focused on the use
of force . N or should it be. While officers must be adequately armed to defend themselves and others, their priority is engaging with their communities: responding to
emergency calls, stopping crime, rendering first aid and
emergency assistance, ensuring the safe exercise of First
Amendment rights, and the like. But the presence of AR-
15s and similar weapons increasingly requires police officers to prepare for their shifts with the understanding
that, at any moment, they might be required to respond
to a shooter equipped with an extraordinarily powerful rifle. The natural response to that dynamic is for officers to
increase their own firepower . Nobody benefits when law
enforcement officers are forced into bearing the equipment that can frighten communities and distance police
officers from the people they serve.
1. When law enforcement needs to increase its firepower and wear more armor just to patrol the streets, the
result is a deeply troubling arms race.
As discussed, ordinary police equipment is no match
for AR-15s. Officers are vulnerable to attack and unable
to effectively respond to shootings perpetrated by criminals with AR-15s using standard-issue equipment. Unsurprisingly, as “criminally minded individuals” have wielded
“high-capacity” semiautomatic weapons “for use against
the public or the police” to tragic results, countless “agen-

cies have transitioned to these firearms in response.”58 To
be adequately prepared, “officers on the street must have
gear that matches the threat.”59 So increasingly, police departments are arming officers with AR -15s as either primary or secondary patrol rifles. 60 They also tap the
Department of Defense’s law enforcement support office
program, 10 U.S.C. §  2576a, to stockpile surplus military
equipment, including “armored vehicles, battle-dress uniforms, helicopters, ballistic helmets, and body armor.”61
The result is an increasingly armed police force, whose
officers are incentivized to don the extremely intimidating
equipment that is necessary to defend themselves against
the rifle that could be awaiting them around any corner or
at the destination of any emergency call.

test of time: law enforcement at its best “ gives reality to
